name: Theophile 'Theo' Dorsainville
languages: Some Army Tagalog and some Army Pidgin, from New Guinea
equipment: Leather jacket, brown, over a welder's wool shirt with burn holes in the cuffs

.32 pocket pistol, an old one with the bluing worn off, 8 rounds loaded, which he keeps in a cigar box at the hall and carries only when he has decided the risk of being searched by a policeman is smaller than the risk of not having it
His welder's hood, gloves and a chipping hammer, in a canvas bag, because he still means to work
A cigar box at the hall on North Roman Street containing the saved pay envelopes of sixty-one welders, three years of them, every one stamped HELPER
A notebook of names: welders, helpers, their wives, their addresses, how much each man is owed, worked out to the penny
A voter registration receipt from the Orleans Parish registrar's office, January 1946, which took him four attempts and an argument about the Constitution
Business cards (100) from the Equity Benevolent Association: T. DORSAINVILLE, RECORDING SECRETARY
features: Seen Worse (Ex-Service origin: advantage on saves against being frightened and against the Shaken condition; the first time each combat he is hit by a firearm, he keeps his reaction and any readied action)

Favors Owed (Fixer: a pool of five favors, refilled at the start of each new case. His favors are not owed by City Hall. They are owed by the Seventh Ward: the benevolent associations, the Black precinct workers, the porters at the Custom House and the Criminal Courts, the Tremé Taxi Company, the women who clean the offices on Carondelet Street, and a hundred and forty families whose men he has taught to weld. One favor buys a name, a room, a car, a man released or a file seen for an hour; two buy something big. Every favor spent is one he owes)
Know Everybody (Fixer: proficiency bonus doubled for Persuasion and Streetwise checks)

Read the Room (Fixer, 2nd level: after a minute of conversation, an Insight check against a person's Deception tells him one of their goals, one of their fears, or whether one thing they said was a lie, and who in the room they are most afraid of)

Circle: City Hall (Fixer, 3rd level: once per case, a city-level favor costs one less. In his case it is the side door of City Hall: the clerks, porters and janitors who see every file and are never seen)

Fast Talk (Fixer, 5th level: as an action, a creature that can hear and understand him makes a WIS save, DC 14, or hesitates, losing its next reaction and having disadvantage on its next attack roll; his favor pool increases by one)

Hiring Hall (Dockworker background: he knows the waterfront and the yards, which foreman picks which men and why; he can get onto any working pier or yard as if he belonged there, and the men who run the waterfront know his face)

personality.traits: I speak slowly and finish my sentences. I write everything down. I do not raise my voice to a white man in public, and I do not lower my eyes either, and I have practised the difference.
personality.ideals: We did the work. We did it right, and men are alive in the Pacific because our welds held. We want the money we earned and the name we earned. Not charity. Wages.
personality.bonds: The sixty-one. Every man and the three women on that list, and their families. The Equity Benevolent Association and its hall, which my grandfather helped build. Octave Mercier, my dead friend's brother.
personality.flaws: I have been patient for so long that I no longer know whether patience is a strategy or a habit. I do not trust white men, and I am going to have to, and I resent it. I am proud, and I will refuse a deal that would help my people if it is offered as a kindness.

appearance: A big, deliberate, dark-skinned man of thirty-eight with grey coming in at the temples, a heavy jaw, burn scars across the backs of both hands and forearms from fifteen years of welding, and reading glasses he puts on to look at paper and takes off to look at people. He dresses for work even when there is none.
backstory: Theophile Dorsainville was born in 1907 on North Roman Street in the Seventh Ward, the son of a Creole carpenter and a laundress, and he learned arc welding in 1929 at a garage on Claiborne Avenue from a man who had learned it in France in the first war. He was the best welder anyone in the Seventh Ward had seen, and for ten years no shipyard in New Orleans would hire him as one. When the war came and the yards needed every pair of hands, Ste. Claire Marine Ways hired him in 1942, and more than a hundred other Black men and women like him, and put them on the hulls of the Navy's lighters and tugs, where they did first-class welding by the Navy's own inspection standards, and it paid them all as helpers: seventy-eight cents an hour against the dollar-twenty the white welders made for the same seam on the same hull. Theo went into the Army in 1943 with an aviation engineer battalion, built airstrips in New Guinea under fire, came home in 1945 a staff sergeant, and went straight back to the yard. In January 1946, with the Navy contracts finished, the yard laid off every Black welder it had. Theo had kept his pay envelopes; and since 1942, on his instruction, so had sixty other men and women. He is the recording secretary of the Equity Benevolent Association, and he has been trying for two months to get a lawyer, a union, the Fair Employment Practice Committee or the Navy to look at those envelopes. Last week, for the first time, someone from inside the yard came to him: Marcel Fontenot, the white pay clerk, who said he had the other half of the proof and would bring it Friday. On Friday Marcel was in the canal.

dmNotes.roleplaying: Theo is the heart of the case and the man with the most at stake, and he is never a helper to the party. He is a principal with his own goal: back wages for sixty-one welders (about $187,000), and a clause in any sale of the yard that the next owner will rate Black welders as welders. He does not need to be rescued, and the GM should never write a scene in which he does. He holds half the proof (Clues D1 and D5's confirmation), and he will not hand it to white investigators for nothing, because every white man who has offered to help him has wanted the envelopes and not the welders. He wants a deal: what will the party do with the proof, and who will be in the room when it is used? He will join the party if they come to him honestly (ideally with Octave), and he will fight beside them on North Roman Street in cs-scenario-002 and on the parade route in cs-scenario-003, where his welders carry the flambeaux for the Krewe of Oneiros for a dollar and a half and the coins the crowd throws at their feet.
dmNotes.voice: Deep, slow, exact. He finishes every sentence, does not use contractions when he is angry, and quotes figures to the penny. With friends in the hall he switches into Creole French and laughs; with white strangers he is formal, polite and impossible to hurry.
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: the back wages, and a written promise that his people will be rated as what they are. Secondary: that Marcel Fontenot, who came to him, is not forgotten as a drunk. Tertiary: stay alive and out of Captain Lebeau's jail long enough to see it, and register forty more voters in the Seventh Ward before the next election.
dmNotes.secrets: Marcel Fontenot told Theo on Monday 25 February that he would bring the Navy-copy pay summaries to the hall on Friday, and that he was going to meet "a Navy commander who can make them listen" first. Theo told him not to trust any officer he had not met. Theo has carried that conversation ever since, and thinks he should have stopped Marcel. Second: Theo knows that the ghost gang, "colored labor gang No. 9", never existed, because he knew every Black worker on the yard by name, and he has a list of the hundred and forty names on gang No. 9 that he copied from a pay sheet in 1944 when a clerk left it on a counter. Several of the names belong to men who were overseas or dead. That list is Clue D5's second source.
dmNotes.attitude: Toward the party: wary, courteous, testing. He warms to anyone who asks what the welders want before asking what the welders have. Toward Octave: trust, and a protective grief. Toward Zélie: affection; he knew her as a girl in her father's shop. Toward Wade Robichaux: he remembers him, a rigger who said nothing in 1941, and he will say so, once. Toward Det. Lamarque: polite suspicion of the badge. Toward Lt. Whitcombe: he will test whether the Navy cares about wages or only about refunds. Toward Yvonne Ste. Claire: none, until she earns some.
